country.name: Portugal
country.summary: Portugal is a narrow country with the Atlantic along its whole western edge, so its wine is a gradient: drenched granite in the Minho, where Vinho Verde is light and sharp; a wall of mountains behind which the Douro bakes on schist and makes Port; granite plateaux in the Dão; cold clay in Bairrada; the windy coast around Lisbon; the hot plains of the Alentejo; and, far out at sea, Madeira. It grows more native grapes than any country its size, led by Touriga Nacional, and names Tempranillo twice, Tinta Roriz in the north and Aragonez in the south. The law stacks DOC above Vinho Regional above plain Vinho, and its label words promise ripeness and age in a way an exam asks about: Reserva is a vintage and half a degree more alcohol, Garrafeira adds time in wood and bottle. The exam's weight falls on the Douro and on Port's two families, Ruby and Tawny.
country.overview:
Portugal's wine story begins with the sea. The country is long and thin, with the ocean down the whole of its western side, and the mountains that run parallel to the coast decide which places are wet and green and which are hot and dry. The Minho in the north-west takes the Atlantic full on and is among the wettest wine regions in Europe; the Serra do Marão stops that weather, and the Douro behind it is a sun trap of schist terraces. The Caramulo and the Serra da Estrela ring the granite of the Dão. South of the Tejo the land flattens into the Alentejo's cork oak plains, where summer is rainless. The islands are separate worlds: Madeira a volcanic rock in the subtropical Atlantic, the Azores further out still.

The trade shaped the north. Port was born of England's wars with France: the Methuen Treaty of 1703 gave Portuguese wine a tariff advantage, the shippers of Porto built an industry on the Douro's wine, and in 1756 the Marquis of Pombal demarcated the valley and put its trade under a chartered company, which makes the Douro one of the first regulated wine regions in the world. A second wave of demarcation in 1907 and 1908 named Vinho Verde, Dão, Colares, Carcavelos, Setúbal and Madeira. Then came decades of stagnation, co-operatives and bulk, until Portugal joined the European Community in 1986 and its DOC system, its regional wines and a new generation of estates took shape.

The law has three floors. DOC, Denominação de Origem Controlada, the European DOP, is the top: around thirty of them, each with a regional commission, a list of grapes and a tasting panel. Vinho Regional is the IGP, fourteen broad areas such as Minho, Duriense, Terras do Dão, Beira Atlântico, Lisboa, Tejo, Península de Setúbal and Alentejano, with a longer list of grapes and looser rules, and plain Vinho sits below. Alongside the origin words run the quality words: Reserva asks for a stated vintage and half a degree of alcohol above the regional minimum; Colheita Seleccionada is a vintage selection with its own higher alcohol floor; Garrafeira alone is an ageing term, thirty months for a red of which twelve are in bottle, twelve months for a white of which six are in bottle.

The exam leans on the Douro and on Port above everything else, then on Vinho Verde's style and the Alvarinho of Monção e Melgaço, on Madeira's four noble grapes in order of sweetness, and on the signatures of the Dão, Bairrada and the Alentejo. Learn the grapes by their homes: Touriga Nacional everywhere, Baga in Bairrada, Encruzado in the Dão, Castelão on sand in the south, Alicante Bouschet with its red flesh in the Alentejo, Arinto for acid that survives heat, and the double name of Tempranillo. Portugal also grows around half of the world's cork, most of it in the Alentejo, which is why a cork question so often has a Portuguese answer.
ladder: Denominação de Origem Controlada, the European DOP: the top tier, a demarcated region with its own grape list, yields and tasting approval, run by a regional commission (CVR), or for Port and Madeira by the IVDP and IVBAM.

The regional wine tier: fourteen broad areas, among them Minho, Duriense, Terras do Dão, Beira Atlântico, Lisboa, Tejo, Península de Setúbal, Alentejano and Algarve, with wider grape lists and room for international varieties.
Wine with no geographical claim, the old vinho de mesa; it may name a grape and a vintage under the European rules.
labels: Not an ageing word: a stated vintage and at least half a degree of alcohol above the regional minimum, so it promises ripeness and selection.

The ageing word: a red matured at least thirty months with twelve in bottle, a white at least twelve months with six in bottle, plus the Reserva alcohol margin. In Port it is a rare style of Niepoort's, cask then large glass demijohns.
A selected harvest: a vintage-dated wine held to a higher alcohol floor than the ordinary wine, close to Reserva in meaning.
The harvest, so the vintage on a still wine; on a Port label it names the single-harvest tawny.
Estate: quinta in the north, herdade for the big farms of the Alentejo, casa and paço for a manor house.
Grape variety; castas is the plural on a back label.
Fortified wine: Port, Madeira, Moscatel de Setúbal, Carcavelos.
Bottled at the estate; engarrafado por names the bottler.
Old vines, often a mixed field blend in the Douro or the Dão.
Literally mature: the old word for any still wine that is not Vinho Verde.
A winery or cellar; Adega Cooperativa is a co-operative.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: The national red: perfumed with violets and bergamot, deep in colour, firm in tannin, the backbone of Port and of dry Douro and Dão reds, now planted in every region.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.styles: The Douro's most planted grape, late ripening, floral and softer than its namesake, the flesh of a Port blend.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Tinta Roriz in the Douro and the Dão, Aragonez in the Alentejo and Lisboa: one grape under two Portuguese names, bringing fruit and body to blends.

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.styles: Bairrada's grape: small berries, high acid and tannin, cherry and tobacco, ageing for decades and the base of its sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The sandy south's red, also called Periquita: raspberry and leather, the grape of the Setúbal peninsula, the Tejo and Lisboa.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.styles: Tinta Amarela in the Douro: spicy, rot-prone, at home in the dry Alentejo.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.styles: A teinturier with red flesh and red juice, French by birth and Portuguese by adoption in the Alentejo, where it gives colour and depth.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.styles: A deep-coloured, soft red of the Dão and Bairrada, valued in blends for fruit and balance.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.styles: Jaen in the Dão: Galicia's fragrant red across the border, early ripening and lighter in tannin.

grapes.name: Alvarinho
grapes.styles: The Albariño of Galicia under its Portuguese name: the fuller, more serious white of Vinho Verde, at its best in Monção e Melgaço.

grapes.name: Loureiro
grapes.styles: Vinho Verde's floral, laurel-scented white, the grape of the Lima valley.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid keeper: crisp, citrus whites that hold their nerve in the heat, the grape of Bucelas, called Pedernã in Vinho Verde.

grapes.name: Encruzado
grapes.styles: The Dão's noble white: textured, mineral, takes oak and age like a white Burgundy.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: Portugal's most planted white, Maria Gomes in Bairrada: aromatic, soft, the base of much Tejo and Lisboa white and of sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Antão Vaz
grapes.styles: The Alentejo's white, heat tolerant and full, from Vidigueira.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Setúbal, the Muscat of Alexandria, makes the fortified wine of the Setúbal peninsula; Moscatel Galego, the small-berried Muscat, makes Moscatel do Douro at Favaios.

grapes.name: Tinta Negra
grapes.styles: Madeira's workhorse red grape, the base of most blended and age-indicated Madeira.

exam: The three floors: DOC, Vinho Regional, Vinho, and which word is Portugal's IGP.
Reserva against Garrafeira: one is ripeness, the other is time, and only Garrafeira demands months in bottle.
The two names of Tempranillo, Tinta Roriz in the north and Aragonez in the south.
Port's two families, Ruby and Tawny, with Vintage, LBV and Colheita placed correctly.
Madeira's four noble grapes from dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey.
The home of each signature grape: Baga, Encruzado, Alvarinho, Castelão, Alicante Bouschet.
The dates that anchor the story: 1703, 1756, 1908, 1986.
traps: Vinho Verde means young wine, not green wine, and it can be red, rosé or sparkling as well as white.
Reserva in Portugal is not a time word; Garrafeira is, and it is nothing like the Spanish Gran Reserva in its minimums.
Colheita on a Port is a tawny from one harvest, aged in wood; a Vintage Port is a ruby from one harvest, aged in bottle.
A tawny's 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years is an indication of the blend's average age, never a vintage.
Moscatel de Setúbal is Muscat of Alexandria; the Douro's Moscatel Galego is the small-berried Muscat.
Alicante Bouschet is a French teinturier, not a Portuguese native, however much the Alentejo has adopted it.
The Douro is a river and a region in Portugal; the same river is the Duero in Spain, where Ribera del Duero grows Tempranillo.

cards.f: Reserva on a Portuguese still wine means what?
cards.b: A stated vintage and at least half a degree of alcohol above the regional minimum: a promise of ripeness, not of age.
Red: thirty months, twelve of them in bottle. White: twelve months, six in bottle. Plus the Reserva alcohol margin.
Tinta Roriz in the Douro and the Dão; Aragonez in the Alentejo and the south.

cards.f: Which Portuguese region was demarcated in 1756, and by whom?
cards.b: The Douro, by the Marquis of Pombal, through the chartered Alto Douro company.
Vinho Verde, Dão, Colares, Carcavelos, Setúbal and Madeira.
Vinho Regional: fourteen broad areas such as Minho, Duriense, Lisboa, Tejo and Alentejano.

cards.f: A teinturier grape at home in the Alentejo
cards.b: Alicante Bouschet, red-fleshed with red juice, French by origin.
Portugal grows around half of the world's cork, most of it on the oak plains of the Alentejo.

questions.q: Which tier stands at the top of Portugal's wine classification?
questions.exp: DOC, Denominação de Origem Controlada, is the European DOP and the top floor. Vinho Regional is the IGP beneath it, Vinho is the floor with no geographical claim, and IPR was a former intermediate tier for regions on their way to DOC.

questions.q: Tinta Roriz and Aragonez are two Portuguese names for which grape?
questions.exp: Both are Tempranillo: Tinta Roriz in the Douro and the Dão, Aragonez in the Alentejo. Mencía has a Portuguese name too, Jaen, but only in the Dão.

questions.q: What are the minimum ageing requirements for a red wine labelled Garrafeira?
questions.exp: Garrafeira is Portugal's one true ageing word: a red needs thirty months with twelve in bottle, a white twelve months with six in bottle. The oak-based minimums belong to Spain's Reserva and Gran Reserva.

questions.q: Beyond a stated vintage, what does the word Reserva require of a Portuguese still wine?
accept: Half a degree more alcohol than the minimum
half a per cent more alcohol
questions.ans: Half a degree more alcohol than the minimum
questions.exp: Reserva is a ripeness word, not a time word: the wine must carry a vintage and at least half a degree of alcohol above the region's minimum. Garrafeira is the term that adds months in wood and bottle.

questions.q: Which Portuguese region was demarcated and regulated in 1756?
questions.exp: The Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro in 1756 and placed the Port trade under a chartered company, which makes it one of the first regulated wine regions anywhere. Vinho Verde, the Dão and the others waited until 1908.

questions.q: Which red grape with red-fleshed berries is widely grown in the Alentejo?
questions.exp: Alicante Bouschet is a teinturier, one of the few grapes whose juice is red, and the Alentejo has made a French crossing its own. Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Tinta Barroca are white-fleshed like almost every other red grape.

questions.q: Which Portuguese region is the home of the white grape Encruzado?
questions.exp: Encruzado belongs to the granite of the Dão, where it makes textured, ageworthy whites. Bairrada's whites are Bical and Maria Gomes, the Alentejo's is Antão Vaz, and Vinho Verde's are Alvarinho and Loureiro.

questions.q: What is the Portuguese name for the IGP tier of wine?
questions.exp: Vinho Regional is the regional wine tier beneath DOC, Portugal's form of the European IGP, with fourteen areas such as Minho, Duriense, Lisboa and Alentejano and a wider list of permitted grapes.

regions.name: Vinho Verde
regions.summary: Vinho Verde is the Minho, Portugal's far north-west between the Minho river on the Spanish border and the Douro, the wettest wine country in the land. Granite, rain and high training make a wine that is light, sharp, low in alcohol and faintly prickly, bottled young: verde means young, not green, and it can be red or rosé as well as white. The region was demarcated in 1908 and holds nine sub-regions named for its rivers and towns. Monção e Melgaço, inland on the Minho in the hills' rain shadow, is the home of Alvarinho and the serious tier; Loureiro leads in the Lima valley; the inky, tart red is Vinhão. The IGP that covers it is Vinho Regional Minho.

terroir.climate: Cool, humid and Atlantic. Weather arrives off the ocean and the rainfall is among the heaviest of any European vineyard, commonly above 1,200 millimetres a year and well beyond that in the hills, much of it in autumn and winter. Winters are mild, summers warm rather than hot, and humidity, mildew and rot are the grower's daily enemies. Inland, up the Minho at Monção and Melgaço, the hills of the Peneda shelter the valley: it is drier and warmer, swings more between day and night, and ripens Alvarinho to twelve or thirteen per cent where the coast struggles past ten.
terroir.soils: Granite almost everywhere, weathered into coarse, sandy, acidic topsoil that drains fast and is poor in nutrients, which is the counterweight to the rain. Towards the south and east, around Baião and Amarante where the region meets the Marão and the Douro, bands of schist appear, and the river valleys carry alluvium. The low fertility and the acidity of the soil are part of why the wines stay light.
terroir.topography: A green, crowded country of hills and river valleys rising from the coast towards the Peneda-Gerês mountains in the north-east and the Serra do Marão in the south-east, which wall it off from the inland. Vineyards run from near sea level to a few hundred metres, nearly all in small family plots on the slopes and valley floors, historically planted around the edges of fields that grew maize beneath them.
terroir.water: The Minho forms the northern border with Galicia; across it lie O Rosal and Condado do Tea of Rías Baixas, and the same grape is Albariño there and Alvarinho here. The Lima, Cávado and Ave run west to the Atlantic, the Sousa and the Paiva into the Douro, and those five rivers give five sub-regions their names; the Tâmega runs through Basto and Amarante to the Douro, which bounds the south at Baião. The ocean keeps the climate mild and wet.

grapes.name: Alvarinho
grapes.styles: The region's serious white, thick-skinned and sure of ripening in Monção e Melgaço: twelve to thirteen per cent, peach, citrus and a stony edge, no spritz, sometimes lees or oak, and able to age a few years.

grapes.name: Loureiro
grapes.styles: The floral workhorse, named for the laurel its scent recalls, at home in the Lima valley: lime blossom, orange peel and bright acidity, the lead grape of most good blends.

grapes.name: Trajadura
grapes.styles: Soft, fuller and lower in acid, the classic partner that rounds Alvarinho and Loureiro; Treixadura across the river.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: Called Pedernã here: acidity and citrus for the blends, and the grape that keeps the cheapest wines fresh.

grapes.name: Avesso
grapes.styles: The grape of Baião in the warmer south-east, fuller and more peachy, making the roundest whites of the region and a few varietal wines.

grapes.name: Azal
grapes.styles: A late, high-acid white of Basto and Amarante, lean and green-appled, mostly for blending.

grapes.name: Vinhão
grapes.styles: The red grape, a teinturier with red flesh: opaque purple, foaming, sharp and drying, drunk young and cold from a ceramic bowl with pork; Sousão in the Douro.

grapes.name: Espadeiro
grapes.styles: A pale, fruity red used mostly for the region's rosé.

wines.note: Pale, light at nine to eleven per cent, bone dry to just off dry, green apple, lime and a faint prickle; serve very cold with grilled sardines, salt cod fritters, clams or oysters. The glass pour and the wine most people mean by the name.

wines.style: Vinho Verde Alvarinho and Monção e Melgaço
wines.note: The serious tier: fuller, twelve to thirteen per cent, peach, grapefruit and wet stone, no spritz, often with lees contact and sometimes a little oak; good with richer fish, roast chicken and Asian food, and it keeps for several years.
A varietal from the Lima valley and elsewhere: floral, laurel and citrus, light and lifted, a fine aperitif and a match for ceviche and salads.
Vinhão's wine, opaque purple with a pink foam, tart and tannic, served chilled in a bowl with rojões, fried pork, in its own tavernas; a trivia point for the exam and a shock for an unprepared guest.
Rosés from Espadeiro and Vinhão, and sparkling wines, the best by the traditional method, from Alvarinho or Loureiro, both small categories that show the region's acidity to advantage.

made.viticulture: The old Minho vineyard was a hedge, not a field: vines trained high on granite posts and wires in the ramada, a pergola, or run up trees, the enforcado, around the margins of plots that grew maize and cabbages beneath them. Height kept the fruit in the wind and away from the damp ground, and gave the family its vegetables; it also gave enormous yields and thin, acid wine. Modern vineyards use the cruzeta, a cross-armed post with the vine trained along wires two metres up, or ordinary cordons on lower trellises, with the canopy opened to dry the bunches. Granite and rain still set the rules: mildew and botrytis are constant, spraying is frequent, and the harvest in September is a race between ripeness and the autumn rains. Holdings are tiny, the minifúndio of the north, so co-operatives and big brands buy from thousands of growers. Monção e Melgaço is the exception in every sense: warmer, drier, planted mostly to Alvarinho on terraces and slopes above the river, and picked riper.
made.winemaking: The prickle that defines the wine was once an accident: wines bottled young went through malolactic fermentation in bottle and kept the carbon dioxide. Today the rule allows a measured dose of carbon dioxide at bottling, and nearly every commercial Vinho Verde is made in stainless steel, fermented cold with cultured yeast, malolactic blocked to keep the acidity, and bottled within months with a few grams of residual sugar to soften the edge. Alcohol is kept low by picking early and by the character of the grapes, and the standard category is capped by law. Alvarinho and the better sub-region wines are made like any serious white: riper fruit, no added gas, lees contact for texture and, from some houses, barrel fermentation or a year in old wood. The red Vinhão is fermented fast on its skins, often in the open, and bottled unfiltered so that it foams in the glass. The best sparkling wines use the traditional method.

law.classification: The Região Demarcada dos Vinhos Verdes was created by law in 1908, one of the demarcations that followed the Douro's by a century and a half, and today it is DOC Vinho Verde under its own commission, the CVRVV, with Vinho Regional Minho as the IGP around it. The DOC is divided into nine sub-regions whose names may appear on the label: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva. The grape list is long, with Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto, Avesso and Azal as the whites that matter and Vinhão, Espadeiro, Borraçal and Padeiro among the reds. Alcohol is written into the rules: the plain category is held to a low ceiling that the Alvarinho and sub-region wines may pass. Alvarinho's name was once Monção e Melgaço's alone on a DOC label; Portaria 152/2015 widened the use of the grape's name across the region and left the sub-region its exclusive claim to Vinho Verde Alvarinho until 2021, and Portaria 333/2016 added the optional mention Origem do Alvarinho for its wines.
tiers: DOC Vinho Verde
The whole demarcated region from the Minho to the Douro, demarcated in 1908: light wines of the listed grapes, the plain category held low in alcohol by rule.
Vinho Verde with a sub-region
One of the nine sub-regions on the label, Monção e Melgaço above all; the wine must come from that sub-region and its recommended grapes and may carry more alcohol than the plain category.
Vinho Verde Alvarinho
The single-varietal wine from Alvarinho, reserved to Monção e Melgaço until the 2015 ordinance's transition ended in 2021; it carries more alcohol than the plain category.
Vinho Verde Espumante
Sparkling wine from the region's grapes, the best by the traditional method.
Vinho Regional Minho
The IGP for the same territory: wider grape list, fuller wines, and the home of many varietal Alvarinhos from outside the sub-region before 2021.
labels: Young, not green: the wine is meant for the year after harvest.
White, red, rosé; the red is Vinhão and the rosé usually Espadeiro.
A producer's selection, a step above the basic blend, not a legal ageing term.
A selected harvest, vintage dated, with a higher alcohol floor.
Needle: a wine with a prickle of gas, the Vinho Verde style in a word.
Estate and manor house, the names of the better family wines.
The regional wine of the same land.

places.name: Monção e Melgaço
places.note: The north-eastern sub-region along the Minho opposite Galicia, sheltered by the hills of the Peneda so that it is warmer and drier than the coast. It is the home of Alvarinho, the one sub-region the exam asks by name, and the source of the region's fullest and longest-lived whites; the varietal wines that made the grape famous came from here in the 1970s.

places.name: Monção
places.note: The riverside town whose co-operative, the Adega de Monção, and whose manor house Palácio da Brejoeira put varietal Alvarinho on the map; the flat lands near the river and the slopes behind are all Alvarinho.

places.name: Melgaço
places.note: Portugal's northernmost municipality, higher and hillier up the Minho, where the small estates that lead the modern Alvarinho movement are based; the terraces climb towards the Peneda.

places.name: Lima
places.note: The valley of the Lima river around Ponte de Lima, west of Monção, and the heartland of Loureiro: floral, lifted whites, some old pergola vineyards, and a handful of estates making Loureiro with lees and age.

places.name: Cávado and Ave
places.note: The two central sub-regions nearest Braga and the coast, wet and populous, where thousands of small growers feed the co-operatives and the big blends; Loureiro, Arinto and Trajadura whites, with Vinhão for the reds.

places.name: Sousa
places.note: Around Penafiel and Paredes in the south, the base of the region's largest house and its best-known brand; Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso whites and plenty of Vinhão red.

places.name: Basto
places.note: The inland eastern sub-region on the Tâmega around Celorico de Basto, the most continental and the last to pick, where Azal keeps its acidity and the reds are sharp.

places.name: Amarante
places.note: On the Tâmega below the Marão, warmer than the coast, growing Avesso and Azal for fuller whites and Vinhão for red; the town itself is the border town between the Minho and the Douro road.

places.name: Baião
places.note: The south-eastern corner on the Douro's north bank, the warmest and driest sub-region, part schist, and the home of Avesso: the roundest whites in Vinho Verde and the only ones that can read like a Douro white.

places.name: Paiva
places.note: A small sub-region south across the Douro around Castelo de Paiva, better known for red Vinhão than for whites.

places.name: Vinho Regional Minho
places.note: The IGP that shares the DOC's territory: the home of fuller, international-leaning whites and, until the 2021 transition ended, of the varietal Alvarinhos grown outside Monção e Melgaço.

producers.name: Anselmo Mendes
producers.why: The Melgaço house that showed Alvarinho could be serious: single-vineyard, lees-aged and barrel-fermented bottlings that set the grape's benchmark.

producers.name: Quinta de Soalheiro
producers.why: A Melgaço family estate that bottled the first Alvarinho from the municipality in 1982 and became the grape's most widely poured name abroad.

producers.name: Palácio da Brejoeira
producers.why: The Monção manor whose varietal Alvarinho from the 1970s made the grape's reputation before anyone else bottled it.

producers.name: Adega de Monção
producers.why: The Monção co-operative whose Alvarinho and Trajadura blend is the honest, cheap face of the sub-region.

producers.name: Aveleda
producers.why: The Penafiel house in the Sousa sub-region behind Casal Garcia, launched in 1939 and one of the biggest brands of Vinho Verde in the world.

producers.name: Quinta do Ameal
producers.why: A Lima valley estate that proved Loureiro could be made with lees and oak and age for years.

producers.name: Aphros
producers.why: A biodynamic Lima estate known for Loureiro, Vinhão and the region's early pét-nat sparkling wines.

producers.name: Quinta de Covela
producers.why: A Baião estate on the Douro's bank that gave Avesso a serious varietal wine.

exam: Define the style in a breath: light, high acid, low alcohol, a prickle, bottled young; verde means young.
Name the grapes by colour: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto (Pedernã), Avesso and Azal for white; Vinhão for red.
Place Monção e Melgaço on the Minho in the rain shadow and tie Alvarinho to it.
Know the nine sub-regions exist and name the ones the exam uses: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Baião.
Hold the Spanish pairing: Albariño, Rías Baixas, Condado do Tea across the river.
Know the IGP, Vinho Regional Minho, and the soil, granite.
Explain the high training and why: rain, rot, and a field of maize underneath.
traps: Verde is young, not green: the colour of the wine is not the point, and red Vinho Verde exists.
The spritz is not a sparkling wine; espumante is a separate category made by the traditional method.
Alvarinho is Albariño, not Loureiro; Loureiro is Loureira in Galicia and Trajadura is Treixadura.
Vinhão is Sousão in the Douro: one teinturier grape, two names.
The region's IGP is Minho, not Vinho Verde; the sub-region is Monção e Melgaço, not Monção alone.

The old note that Alvarinho may only be labelled from Monção e Melgaço is out of date: the 2015 ordinance opened the grape's name to the region, with the sub-region's exclusivity on the varietal label ending with the 2021 transition.

cards.f: What does verde mean in Vinho Verde?
cards.b: Young, not green: a wine meant to be drunk within a year of harvest. It can be white, red, rosé or sparkling.

cards.f: Vinho Verde: climate and soil in a breath
cards.b: Cool, very wet Atlantic; granite weathered to acid sand. High training lifts the fruit above the damp.
Monção e Melgaço, on the Minho river in the north-east, sheltered and drier than the coast.

cards.f: The white grapes of Vinho Verde
cards.b: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto (called Pedernã), Avesso and Azal.

cards.f: The red grape of Vinho Verde
cards.b: Vinhão, a teinturier: opaque purple, tart, foaming, drunk cold from a bowl. It is Sousão in the Douro.

cards.f: How many sub-regions does DOC Vinho Verde name?
cards.b: Nine: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva, most of them named for rivers.

cards.f: The river that borders Spain in Vinho Verde
cards.b: The Minho. Rías Baixas lies across it, where Alvarinho is Albariño.

cards.f: The IGP of the Vinho Verde region
cards.b: Vinho Regional Minho.
The Lima, around Ponte de Lima.
Once malolactic fermentation in bottle; now a measured dose of carbon dioxide allowed at bottling.

questions.q: Which sub-region of Vinho Verde is the home of varietal Alvarinho?
questions.exp: Monção e Melgaço sits inland on the Minho river in the shelter of the Peneda hills, drier and warmer than the coast, and Alvarinho ripens there. Lima is Loureiro country, Baião grows Avesso and Basto is the cool inland sub-region.

questions.q: Which grape makes the opaque, tart red Vinho Verde?
questions.exp: Vinhão is a teinturier with red flesh and gives the foaming purple red drunk cold from bowls; it is Sousão in the Douro. Espadeiro is mostly for rosé, Baga belongs to Bairrada and Castelão to the sandy south.

questions.q: How many sub-regions does DOC Vinho Verde contain?
questions.exp: Nine: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva, most of them named for rivers. The Dão, for comparison, has seven.

questions.q: Which rock underlies most of the vineyards of Vinho Verde?
questions.exp: Granite weathered to coarse acid sand is the soil of the Minho, as it is across the river in Rías Baixas. Schist is the Douro's rock, limestone Bairrada's and basalt Madeira's.

questions.q: What does the word verde mean on a bottle of Vinho Verde?
accept: Green in the sense of young
questions.exp: Verde describes the wine's youth, not a colour: it is made to be drunk within the year, light and fresh, and the category includes red and rosé as well as white.

questions.q: Which Vinho Regional covers the same territory as DOC Vinho Verde?
questions.exp: Vinho Regional Minho is the IGP of the north-west, named for the province and the river; it gives fuller wines and wider grape choices than the DOC, and held the varietal Alvarinhos grown outside Monção e Melgaço before 2021.

questions.q: Which sub-region of Vinho Verde is the heartland of Loureiro?
questions.exp: Loureiro, the laurel-scented white, has its home in the Lima valley west of Monção, where a few estates make varietal wines with lees and age. Alvarinho's home is the neighbouring Monção e Melgaço.

questions.q: Across the Minho river in Spain, Alvarinho is known by which name?
questions.exp: Albariño of Rías Baixas and Alvarinho of Monção e Melgaço are the same grape on two banks of the Minho. Treixadura is Trajadura, Loureira is Loureiro, and Godello is Gouveio in the Douro.

regions.name: Douro / Port
regions.summary: The Douro is the river valley east of Porto, behind the Serra do Marão, where the Atlantic stops and schist terraces climb from the water. Demarcated in 1756, it is one of the oldest regulated wine regions anywhere and the home of Port, a red wine fortified during fermentation to keep its sugar and aged by tradition in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia. Since Barca Velha in 1952, and formally since DOC Douro in 1982, the same grapes make dry wines. Three sub-regions run upstream, Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior, each hotter and drier than the last. Port splits into two families: Ruby, kept from air and aged in bottle, and Tawny, aged in wood.

terroir.climate: Continental with a Mediterranean summer. The Serra do Marão takes the Atlantic rain, so rainfall falls from around 900 millimetres in the Baixo Corgo to under 400 in the Douro Superior, while summer temperatures pass 40 degrees in the gorge and winters are cold. Altitude moderates: the valley floor is hottest and the vineyards climb to 700 metres, where whites and fresher reds now go. Drought and heat, not rot, are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Schist, xisto, a laminated metamorphic rock that splits into near-vertical plates, so roots follow the fissures many metres down to water. It is poor in nutrients, holds the day's heat and gives it back at night. Granite outcrops at the region's edges and on the higher ground, and the vineyard register marks it down, because granite holds less water and makes lighter wine.
terroir.topography: A steep, winding gorge: slopes of 30 degrees are ordinary and some pass 60, which is why the vineyard is terraced. The old socalcos are narrow walled steps built by hand before phylloxera; patamares are the wide bulldozed terraces of the 1970s onward that let a tractor through; vinha ao alto plants rows straight up the gentler slopes. The south-facing north bank is hotter, and every side valley has its own climate.
terroir.water: The Douro rises in Spain as the Duero, forms the border for some way, leaves it at Barca d'Alva at the eastern end of the Douro Superior and runs west for around two hundred kilometres to Porto. The Corgo divides the Baixo Corgo from the Cima Corgo, the Pinhão valley is the heart of the Cima Corgo, and the Cachão da Valeira gorge marks the start of the Douro Superior. The Tua, Torto, Távora, Sabor and Côa are other tributaries a label may name.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Small berries, thick skins, low yields: violets, bergamot, blackberry, deep colour and firm tannin, the grape that structures a Port blend and leads the best dry reds.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.styles: The most planted grape of the Douro, late ripening and reliable on hot sites, floral and juicy, the flesh and the perfume of the blend.

grapes.name: Tinta Roriz
grapes.styles: Tempranillo under its Douro name, Aragonez further south: generous fruit and body, early ripening, best on cooler sites.

grapes.name: Tinta Barroca
grapes.styles: Early ripening and high in sugar, soft and fleshy, planted on cooler, higher or north-facing land so that it keeps its balance.

grapes.name: Tinto Cão
grapes.styles: Low yielding and late, fine-boned with good acidity and long life, prized in small measure for the blend's spine.

grapes.name: Sousão
grapes.styles: A teinturier with red flesh, the Vinhão of Vinho Verde: colour and acidity for Port in a hot year.

grapes.name: Tinta Amarela
grapes.styles: Trincadeira in the south: spicy and aromatic, rot-prone on the coast but at ease in the dry Douro.

grapes.name: Gouveio
grapes.styles: Godello of Galicia: the backbone of the Douro's dry whites and the base of White Port, with Malvasia Fina, Rabigato and Viosinho.

grapes.name: Rabigato
grapes.styles: A high-acid white of the Douro Superior that keeps the dry whites fresh.

grapes.name: Viosinho
grapes.styles: A low-yielding, aromatic white used for the best dry whites from altitude.

grapes.name: Moscatel Galego
grapes.styles: The small-berried Muscat, grown on the Favaios plateau above Pinhão for the fortified Moscatel do Douro.

wines.note: Young, deep red and fruity, a blend of years kept two or three years in large vats and filtered; serve slightly cool with chocolate, blue cheese or a berry dessert. Reserve Ruby is the richer selection.

A single year, kept four to six years in wood and bottled ready to drink, usually filtered so that it needs no decanting; the traditional unfiltered kind throws a deposit and is decanted. Ripe plum and spice at a fraction of a Vintage's price.

The top of the Ruby family: one declared year, bottled unfiltered in its second or third year, then matured for decades in bottle, where it throws a crust. Decant it. Black fruit, violets, firm tannin; Stilton and walnuts are the classic table.
A Vintage Port from one estate, such as Vargellas or Bomfim, often released in the years a house does not declare, and served exactly like a Vintage Port.
Aged in pipes with a little air, so the colour fades to amber and the fruit turns to nuts, dried fig and caramel; a Reserve has real age. Serve cool with crème brûlée, pecan pie or hard cheese.

wines.style: Tawny with an Indication of Age
wines.note: 10, 20, 30 or 40 Years, and since 2022 also 50 Years: the number is an indication of the blend's average age and character, approved by the IVDP's tasting panel, not the age of any one wine. Twenty is the sommelier's sweet spot: walnut, orange peel, toffee.

A tawny from one harvest, aged at least seven years in wood and often far longer, bottled when sold with the bottling date on the label. Single-vintage like a Vintage Port but opposite in character: oxidative, amber, nutty, ready on opening.
From Gouveio, Malvasia Fina, Rabigato and Viosinho, dry to sweet, Lágrima the sweetest; aged whites carry the same indications of age. Served cold, often with tonic and mint as the Douro's aperitif.

Dry wines from the Port grapes, often old-vine field blends: dark, structured, schist-scented, with French oak; the best, from Barca Velha onward, age for decades and sit with lamb, game and grilled meats.
From Gouveio, Rabigato, Viosinho and Arinto grown at altitude: stony, textured, sometimes barrel fermented, and the valley's answer to white Burgundy.

made.viticulture: Every Douro vineyard carries a grade. The cadastro, the vineyard register, scores each plot on altitude, locality, slope, aspect, soil, shelter, vine age, density, yield and grape varieties, and ranks it by letter from A, the best, downward. Each year the IVDP sets the beneficio, the volume of must that may be fortified, and shares it out by grade, so a top plot may turn most of its crop into Port while a poor one sends its grapes to DOC Douro or the regional wine. The terraces tell the region's history: the walled socalcos of the pre-phylloxera vineyard, some abandoned as mortórios after the louse arrived in the 1860s; the bulldozed patamares of the replanting that began in the 1970s; and vinha ao alto, rows straight up the gentler slopes. The old vineyards are mixed field blends of dozens of varieties; the new ones are blocks of the five favoured grapes, Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão, chosen by research in the 1970s and 1980s. Yields are low, heat and drought are the hazards, picking is by hand from mid-September, and the highest land is now planted for whites and freshness.
made.winemaking: Port is made fast. Because fermentation will be stopped after two or three days, colour and tannin must come out quickly, and the valley found ways to do it: foot treading in shallow granite lagares, robotic lagares, autovinifiers and pumping over. When the must has fermented roughly half its sugar, at about six to nine per cent alcohol, it is run off the skins into a vat holding aguardente, grape spirit at 77 per cent, near one part spirit to four of wine. The yeast dies, the sugar stays, and the Port finishes at 19 to 22 per cent with the sweetness of its own grapes. From then on it is a matter of air and time: Ruby, LBV and Vintage are kept in large vats or bottled early to hold their colour, while tawnies live in pipes of around 550 litres in the lodges of Gaia or, since 1986, in the Douro itself, where the heat speeds the ageing. Dry Douro wines ferment to completion, mostly in stainless steel or lagares, and age in French oak; the whites from altitude are often barrel fermented.

law.classification: In 1756 the Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro and gave the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro charge of its trade. Port's institute was founded in 1933 and became the IVDP, the Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto, in 2003; it regulates both DOC Porto and DOC Douro, the dry wine appellation of 1982, with Vinho Regional Duriense as the IGP. Port's categories are defined by the IVDP: Ruby, Reserve, LBV (bottled between the fourth and sixth year after harvest), Crusted (unfiltered, three years in bottle), Vintage (a declared year, bottled in its second or third year), Tawny, Reserve Tawny, tawny with an indication of age (10, 20, 30, 40 and since 2022 50 Years), Colheita (one harvest, at least seven years in wood), White, Rosé and Garrafeira. Port must be made within the region and, since 1986, may be aged and shipped from the Douro as well as from Gaia.
tiers: DOC Porto
Fortified wine of the demarcated Douro, 19 to 22 per cent, made from grapes graded in the cadastro and fortified within the beneficio; the categories above.
DOC Douro
The dry wines of the same region since 1982: red, white and rosé, plus Moscatel do Douro; Barca Velha of 1952 is the ancestor.
Vinho Regional Duriense
The IGP of the valley, for wines that step outside the DOC grape list or rules.
Ruby family
Ruby, Reserve Ruby, LBV, Crusted, Vintage and Single Quinta Vintage: wine kept from air so that it stays red and fruity, the best of it aged in bottle and decanted.
Tawny family
Tawny, Reserve Tawny, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 Years, Colheita: wine aged in wood with air so that it turns amber and nutty, ready when bottled, never decanted.
The three sub-regions
Baixo Corgo, the wettest and most fertile; Cima Corgo around Pinhão, the heart and the home of the great quintas; Douro Superior, the driest and hottest, up to the Spanish border.
labels: An estate; a single quinta Port comes from one farm, often in an undeclared year.
A house's decision, approved by the IVDP, that a year is good enough for a Vintage Port; roughly three years in ten.
A single-harvest tawny, at least seven years in wood, with its bottling date.
10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years on a tawny or white: the blend's average age and style, not a vintage.
An LBV that spent at least three years in bottle before release, the unfiltered style.
Old vines, usually a mixed field blend on the old terraces.
The annual licence to fortify, shared out by vineyard grade.
The vineyard register that grades each plot by letter, A the best.
The warehouse where Port ages, traditionally in Vila Nova de Gaia.
The Port cask, around 550 litres in the Douro, and the unit the trade counts in.

places.name: Baixo Corgo
places.note: The western, downstream sub-region around Peso da Régua, the old river port and administrative town, below the mouth of the Corgo: the wettest and coolest, the most fertile and the highest yielding, the source of much basic Ruby and Tawny and of good dry wine from its higher slopes.

places.name: Cima Corgo
places.note: The central sub-region upstream of the Corgo, centred on Pinhão: steeper, hotter and drier than the Baixo Corgo, home of most of the famous quintas and of the bulk of Vintage Port.

places.name: Pinhão
places.note: The small town at the Pinhão river's mouth whose railway station is tiled with vintage scenes; the great quintas of the shipping houses, Noval and Crasto lie around it on both banks.

places.name: Vale de Mendiz
places.note: A village of old field-blend vineyards above Pinhão, the source of some of the Douro's most celebrated dry reds.

places.name: Douro Superior
places.note: The eastern sub-region from the Valeira gorge to the Spanish border at Barca d'Alva: the hottest, driest and most recently planted, with gentler slopes near the river, the source of Barca Velha and Quinta do Vale Meão.

places.name: Quinta de Vargellas
places.note: A Taylor's estate since 1893, far upriver where the Cima Corgo gives way to the Douro Superior, famous for its single quinta Vintage Port.

places.name: Vila Nova de Gaia
places.note: The town across the river from Porto where the shippers' lodges stand and where by law all Port was aged and shipped until 1986; the names on the roofs are still the houses a guest knows.

places.name: Porto
places.note: The city at the river's mouth that gave the wine its name, Oporto in old English usage; the British shippers' Factory House dates from 1790 and the Port Wine Institute began here in 1933.

producers.name: Taylor Fladgate
producers.why: Founded in 1692, owner of Quinta de Vargellas, maker of the first commercial LBV with its 1965 vintage released in 1970, and a benchmark for firm, long-lived Vintage Port.

producers.name: Fonseca
producers.why: A house of 1815 in the same group as Taylor's, famous for a richer, more opulent Vintage style and for Bin 27 as the Reserve Ruby everyone knows.

producers.name: W. and J. Graham's
producers.why: Founded in 1820 and built on Quinta dos Malvedos since 1890, known for a sweet, generous Vintage style and for its 20 Years tawny.

producers.name: Dow's
producers.why: The driest of the great Vintage styles, built on Quinta do Bomfim at Pinhão and Senhora da Ribeira upstream.

producers.name: Warre's
producers.why: The oldest of the British houses, trading since 1670, with Quinta da Cavadinha and a traditional unfiltered LBV.

producers.name: Niepoort
producers.why: A family house of 1842 famous for Colheitas, for the cask-then-demijohn Garrafeira style and, since the 1990s, for the dry Douro reds that changed the valley's ambitions.

producers.name: Sandeman
producers.why: Founded in 1790, with the caped Don silhouette of 1928 that made it the most recognisable label in Port, strong in LBV and aged tawny.

producers.name: Feist
producers.why: A small nineteenth-century shipper whose long-matured LBVs give a taste of mature Port at a modest price.

producers.name: Quinta do Noval
producers.why: The Pinhão estate whose 1931 made its name and whose Nacional, from a tiny plot of ungrafted vines, is the rarest Vintage Port of all.

producers.name: Casa Ferreirinha
producers.why: The dry-wine house of Ferreira, founded 1751, and the maker of Barca Velha, the first great Douro table wine, from 1952.

producers.name: Quinta do Crasto
producers.why: A Cima Corgo estate between Régua and Pinhão whose single-vineyard old-vine reds, Maria Teresa and Vinha da Ponte, are reference dry Douro.

producers.name: Quinta do Vallado
producers.why: A Baixo Corgo estate near Régua dating from 1716, linked to the Ferreira family, known for dry reds and aged tawnies.

producers.name: Quinta do Vale Meão
producers.why: The Douro Superior estate built by Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira in the 1880s, the source of Barca Velha's grapes for decades and of its own great red since 1999.

producers.name: Wine and Soul
producers.why: A Vale de Mendiz house whose Pintas, from an old field blend, is a modern icon of dry Douro.

producers.name: Croft
producers.why: One of the oldest names in the trade, maker of Quinta da Roêda vintage Ports and the first Rosé Port in 2008.

producers.name: Ramos Pinto
producers.why: A Portuguese house of 1880 known for aged tawnies and for the research that chose the Douro's five favoured grapes.

producers.name: Kopke
producers.why: The oldest Port house, dating from 1638, and a specialist in Colheitas and very old tawnies.

exam: Hold the two families apart: Ruby (fruit, bottle, decant) against Tawny (air, wood, no decanting), and place Vintage, LBV, Crusted and Colheita on the right side.
Know the fortification numbers: 77 per cent spirit, about one part in five, 19 to 22 per cent finished, the ferment stopped at roughly half the sugar.
Know the three sub-regions in order upstream and their characters, with Pinhão at the heart of the Cima Corgo.
Name the five favoured grapes and which is the most planted (Touriga Franca).
The dates: 1703 Methuen, 1756 demarcation, 1933 the institute, 1952 Barca Velha, 1982 DOC Douro, 1986 shipping from the Douro, 2001 World Heritage.
Know the LBV and Vintage bottling windows and the seven years of a Colheita.
Know what the cadastro and the beneficio are and why a grade matters.
Service: decant Vintage and Crusted and unfiltered LBV; pour aged tawny cool; White Port cold.
traps: Colheita and Vintage are both single-year Ports, but Colheita is a wood-aged tawny and Vintage a bottle-aged ruby: opposite wines.
A tawny's 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years is an average-age indication, never a vintage; Colheita is the vintage-dated tawny.
Port is sweet from its own grape sugar, stopped by spirit; nothing is added to sweeten it.
Vintage Port is bottled young, in its second or third year; LBV is bottled later, in its fourth to sixth, which is what Late means.
The most planted grape is Touriga Franca, not Touriga Nacional, however often the latter is named first.
Tinta Roriz is Tempranillo; Sousão is Vinhão; Gouveio is Godello; Tinta Amarela is Trincadeira.
Vila Nova de Gaia is where Port is aged, not where its grapes grow; the vineyard lies about 100 kilometres (sixty miles) upstream behind the Marão.
Douro Superior means upstream and inland, towards Spain, the driest end of the valley, not a superior grade.

cards.b: Ruby: kept from air, red and fruity, Vintage aged in bottle, decanted. Tawny: aged in wood with air, amber and nutty, ready when bottled.
Fermentation stopped at about half the sugar with grape spirit at 77 per cent, roughly one part in five; the wine finishes at 19 to 22 per cent.

cards.f: The three sub-regions, downstream to upstream
cards.b: Baixo Corgo (wettest, fertile), Cima Corgo (Pinhão, the heart), Douro Superior (driest, to the Spanish border).
Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca (the most planted), Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão.

cards.f: LBV and Vintage: the bottling windows
cards.b: LBV: between the fourth and sixth year after harvest. Vintage: in the second or third year, then decades in bottle.
A tawny from a single harvest, at least seven years in wood, labelled with its bottling date. Not a Vintage Port.

cards.f: What a tawny's 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years means
cards.b: An indication of the blend's average age and character, approved by the IVDP's panel, not a vintage. Fifty Years was added in 2022.
1756 demarcation by Pombal; 1933 the Port institute; 1952 Barca Velha; 1982 DOC Douro; 1986 ageing and shipping allowed from the Douro; 2001 World Heritage.
Cadastro: the register grading every plot by letter, A the best. Beneficio: the yearly licence that says how much must may be made into Port, shared out by grade.

cards.f: Where Port is aged by tradition
cards.b: In the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from Porto; since 1986 also in the Douro itself.

questions.q: Which sub-region of the Douro is the driest and reaches the Spanish border?
questions.exp: The Douro Superior runs from the Valeira gorge east to Barca d'Alva on the border, with under 400 millimetres of rain. The Baixo Corgo is the wet western end, the Cima Corgo the heart around Pinhão; Trás-os-Montes is the separate region to the north.

questions.q: In which year was the Douro demarcated by the Marquis of Pombal?
questions.exp: Pombal demarcated the valley in 1756 and put its trade under a chartered company. 1703 is the Methuen Treaty, 1908 the year Vinho Verde, Dão and others were demarcated, and 1986 Portugal's entry into the European Community.

questions.q: Which style of Port comes from a single harvest and is aged at least seven years in wood?
questions.exp: Colheita is the single-harvest tawny, oxidative and amber, bottled with its bottling date. Vintage is bottled in its second or third year, LBV in its fourth to sixth, and Crusted is a blend of years.

questions.q: At what strength is the grape spirit used to fortify Port?
questions.exp: Aguardente at 77 per cent is added when the must has fermented about half its sugar, near one part spirit to four of wine, so the Port finishes at 19 to 22 per cent with its own grape sugar intact.

questions.q: Which town at the mouth of its namesake river is the heart of the Cima Corgo?
questions.exp: Pinhão sits where the Pinhão river meets the Douro, with the great quintas of the Cima Corgo on the slopes around it. Peso da Régua is the town of the Baixo Corgo downstream.

questions.q: Between which years after the harvest must a Late Bottled Vintage Port be bottled?
questions.exp: LBV spends four to six years in wood before bottling, which is why it is Late. Vintage Port is bottled in its second or third year, and seven years is the minimum in wood for a Colheita.

questions.q: What is the name of the annual authorisation that fixes how much must may be made into Port?
questions.exp: The IVDP sets the beneficio each year and shares it out by the cadastro grade of each vineyard, so the best plots may fortify most of their crop and the rest goes to dry Douro wine.

questions.q: Which grape is the most widely planted in the Douro?
questions.exp: Touriga Franca, late ripening and dependable on hot sites, covers more of the valley than any other grape. Touriga Nacional is the most prized but lower yielding, Tinta Roriz is Tempranillo, and Tinto Cão is a small, fine component.

regions.name: Dão
regions.summary: The Dão is a granite plateau in the centre-north of Portugal around the city of Viseu, ringed by mountains that shut out both the Atlantic rain and the inland extremes: the Caramulo to the west, the Serra da Estrela to the south-east. Vineyards sit at 400 to 700 metres in clearings among pine forest, demarcated in 1908, divided into seven sub-regions. Touriga Nacional is said to have been born here, and with Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz it makes fragrant, firm, long-lived reds; Encruzado is Portugal's noblest white. Decades of co-operative rule dulled the region until estates revived it in the 1990s. The IGP is Terras do Dão.

terroir.climate: Temperate and sheltered. Rain is plentiful, around 1,100 millimetres, but falls mostly in winter; summers are warm and dry, with days in the mid thirties and cool nights that the altitude guarantees. The Caramulo and Buçaco hills to the west take the Atlantic weather, the Estrela to the south-east holds off the continental heat and gives spring snowmelt. The result is a slow, even ripening season and reds with freshness that the hotter Douro lacks.
terroir.soils: Granite, weathered into coarse sand the growers call saibro, poor, acidic and free draining, lying over bedrock that forces roots to search. A little schist appears at the southern and western margins. The low fertility holds yields down naturally and the sand keeps the wines fine-boned rather than heavy.
terroir.topography: A high, undulating plateau at 400 to 700 metres, rising towards the Serra da Estrela, Portugal's highest mainland range, in the south-east and dropping towards the Mondego valley. The vineyards are small, walled plots scattered among maritime pine, eucalyptus and granite boulders, never a continuous carpet; the forest shelters them and scents the air.
terroir.water: Three rivers name the region's parts: the Dão itself, which gives the region its name, the Mondego, the longest river entirely within Portugal, which runs south-west through the plateau to Coimbra, and the Alva in the south. Their valleys are the warmer, lower sites; the rivers matter more for the landscape than for the climate.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Claimed as a native of the Dão, from the village of Tourigo near Tondela: here it is floral and fine-boned rather than massive, violets, bergamot and blackberry with firm, ripe tannin, in blends and as a varietal.

grapes.name: Jaen
grapes.styles: Galicia's Mencía under its Dão name: early ripening, red-fruited, supple and lower in tannin, the softener in a Dão blend and a pretty varietal.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.styles: Deeply coloured, soft and strawberry-scented, balancing Touriga's structure in the classic blend.

grapes.name: Tinta Roriz
grapes.styles: Tempranillo, adding fruit and body; it ripens early on the warmer slopes.

grapes.name: Rufete
grapes.styles: A light, high-acid red of the old mixed vineyards, more common towards the Spanish border.

grapes.name: Bastardo
grapes.styles: The Jura's Trousseau under a Portuguese name, pale and high in alcohol, a survivor in old plots.

grapes.name: Encruzado
grapes.styles: The region's great white and nearly its own: textured, mineral, citrus and fennel, takes barrel fermentation and lees like a white Burgundy and ages for ten years.

grapes.name: Bical
grapes.styles: An early, aromatic white shared with Bairrada, for blends and sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Cercial
grapes.styles: A high-acid white of the Beiras for freshness in blends; not Madeira's Sercial.

grapes.name: Malvasia Fina
grapes.styles: A soft, floral white in the traditional blends, called Boal in some places.

wines.note: The classic blend of Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz: medium bodied, fragrant, red and black fruit with pine and earth, fresh acidity and firm, fine tannin, built to age ten or twenty years. Roast kid, lamb and the region's cured meats are its table.
The varietal: violets, bergamot and blackberry with the plateau's freshness, more perfume and less weight than its Douro cousin.
Often barrel fermented and lees aged: textured, citrus and white flowers over wet stone and a hint of fennel, able to age a decade; roast chicken, grilled fish, pork with clams.
Blends of Encruzado, Bical, Cercial and Malvasia Fina, crisp and clean when young, the everyday white of Viseu's tables.
Traditional method sparkling wine from the high, cool vineyards, from Encruzado, Bical and Touriga Nacional; a small category with real acidity.
Pale rosés from Touriga Nacional and Jaen, dry and fresh, for the summer.

made.viticulture: The Dão vineyard is a patchwork. Holdings are small, walled in granite and scattered through the pine forest, often old mixed plantings of a dozen varieties on bush vines or low cordons; the modern estates plant blocks of Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Encruzado on wire-trained vines. Altitude sets the season: budbreak is late enough to dodge most spring frost, summers are dry, and harvest runs from late September into October with the Estrela already cold at night. Poor granite sand keeps yields modest without much help. The hazards are fire in the summer forest and drought in a hot year rather than rot. The region's history is written in its vineyards too: from the 1940s until the end of the 1980s the law channelled growers' grapes into co-operatives, which made the Dão a byword for hard, dull red; after Portugal joined the European Community the estates took back their fruit, and the finest old plots at altitude, in Silgueiros, Senhorim and under the Estrela, became the raw material of the revival.
made.winemaking: Traditional Dão red was fermented with stems in open stone lagares or old wooden vats, left long on its skins, aged for years in large old casks of oak or chestnut and sold firm and dried out. The revival kept the structure and lost the harshness: destemming, gentler extraction in stainless steel or lagar, moderate time in French oak of various sizes, and bottling while the fruit still shows. Many houses keep the old habit of blending four or five grapes, because Touriga Nacional alone can be too austere young and Jaen too soft. Encruzado is the white that justified barrel fermentation in Portugal: whole-bunch pressing, fermentation in oak, lees stirring and a year in wood give a wine of texture and length, though stainless steel versions keep the grape's citrus edge. Sparkling wine is made by the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle.

law.classification: The Dão was demarcated in 1908 and is DOC Dão under its regional commission, the CVR Dão, with Vinho Regional Terras do Dão as the IGP around it. The DOC names seven sub-regions that may appear on the label: Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara and Terras de Senhorim. Reds must be built on the recommended grapes, Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro, Tinta Roriz, Rufete and their companions, and whites on Encruzado, Bical, Cercial, Malvasia Fina and Verdelho; varietal labels follow the national rule. A superior designation, Dão Nobre, exists for wines from the best fruit that meet stricter standards and longer ageing. The usual national terms apply: Reserva for a vintage and extra alcohol, Garrafeira for thirty months with twelve in bottle on a red.
tiers: DOC Dão
The whole plateau demarcated in 1908: reds, whites, rosés and sparkling wines from the region's grapes under the CVR Dão.
Dão with a sub-region
One of the seven sub-regions on the label: Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara or Terras de Senhorim.
Dão Nobre
The superior designation for wines meeting stricter grape, alcohol and ageing standards.
Vinho Regional Terras do Dão
The IGP of the same land, for wines outside the DOC list.
labels: A vintage and half a degree more alcohol than the minimum, as across Portugal.
The ageing term: thirty months with twelve in bottle for a red.
Old vines, usually the mixed plots of the pre-revival vineyard.
The regional wine of the plateau.

places.name: Viseu
places.note: The cathedral city at the centre of the plateau, the seat of the regional commission and the hub from which the sub-regions radiate.

places.name: Silgueiros
places.note: The sub-region south of Viseu along the Dão river, prized for Encruzado and for fine, fragrant reds; many of the revival's single-estate wines come from here.

places.name: Terras de Senhorim
places.note: Around Nelas and Canas de Senhorim in the heart of the plateau, home of the historic manors of Santar and of some of the oldest estates to bottle their own wine.

places.name: Terras de Azurara
places.note: Around Mangualde east of Viseu, with several of the leading modern estates and a reputation for Touriga Nacional.

places.name: Serra da Estrela
places.note: The highest sub-region under the mountains in the south-east, around Seia and Gouveia, with the coolest sites, old vines and the longest, freshest reds; the sheep's cheese of the same name is the region's great table match.

places.name: Besteiros
places.note: The western sub-region at the foot of the Caramulo around Tondela, nearest the Atlantic weather and the claimed cradle of Touriga Nacional at Tourigo.

places.name: Castendo and Alva
places.note: Castendo lies in the north-east around Penalva do Castelo; Alva in the south along its river towards Oliveira do Hospital. Both are small and rarely named on a label.

places.name: Santar
places.note: A village of granite manor houses near Nelas whose estates have bottled Dão under their own names for generations, a landmark of the region's revival.

producers.name: Quinta dos Roques
producers.why: A Mangualde estate whose varietal Touriga Nacional and barrel-fermented Encruzado defined the modern Dão in the 1990s.

producers.name: Quinta da Pellada
producers.why: An old-vine estate under the Serra da Estrela at Seia, with its sister Quinta de Saes, a reference for fine, ageworthy Dão red.

producers.name: Quinta dos Carvalhais
producers.why: The Dão estate of the Sogrape group at Mangualde, widely poured abroad, with a dependable Encruzado.

producers.name: Casa de Santar
producers.why: The historic manor of Santar near Nelas, among the first houses to bottle estate Dão and still a name a guest may know.

producers.name: Casa da Passarella
producers.why: A nineteenth-century estate at Gouveia under the Estrela, revived with old vines and a classical style.

producers.name: Quinta de Cabriz
producers.why: The large Carregal do Sal estate whose reliable reds put Dão by the glass on lists everywhere.

producers.name: Caves São João
producers.why: The Bairrada house whose Porta dos Cavaleiros label kept long-aged traditional Dão alive through the co-operative decades.

exam: Place it: a granite plateau at 400 to 700 metres around Viseu, sheltered by the Caramulo and the Estrela, among pine forest.
Know the red grapes, Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz, and that Jaen is Mencía.
Encruzado is the white the exam wants placed here, and nowhere else.
Know the date, 1908, the seven sub-regions, and the IGP, Terras do Dão.
Know the story: co-operatives from the 1940s, revival after 1986 by estates.
Describe the style: fragrant, fresh, firm, medium bodied, long-lived.
traps: Dão is granite, like Vinho Verde, not schist like the Douro; the climate is the difference between those two granites.
Jaen is Mencía, not a Spanish town's wine; the name is the same as the Andalusian city but the grape is Galician.
Encruzado belongs to the Dão; Arinto is Bucelas and Vinho Verde, Antão Vaz is the Alentejo, Bical is shared with Bairrada.
Touriga Nacional is claimed by the Dão, not the Douro, as its birthplace.
The Dão lies south of the Douro and east of Bairrada, inland; it is not on the coast.
Cercial of the Dão and Bairrada is not Madeira's Sercial.

cards.b: A granite plateau around Viseu at 400 to 700 metres, sheltered by the Caramulo and the Serra da Estrela, vineyards among pine forest.

cards.f: The white grape the exam places in the Dão
cards.b: Encruzado: textured, mineral, barrel fermented at its best, ages ten years.

cards.b: Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara and Terras de Senhorim.
1908, the same year as Vinho Verde, Colares, Carcavelos, Setúbal and Madeira; the Douro had gone first in 1756.

cards.f: Why the Dão went quiet, and when it woke
cards.b: From the 1940s the law pushed grapes into co-operatives; after Portugal joined the European Community in 1986 the estates took their fruit back and revived the region.
The Dão, at the village of Tourigo near Tondela in the Besteiros sub-region.

questions.q: Which white grape is the signature of the Dão?
questions.exp: Encruzado is the Dão's own white, textured and ageworthy. Arinto is Bucelas and the Minho's Pedernã, Alvarinho is Vinho Verde's, and Antão Vaz belongs to the Alentejo.

questions.q: Which range of hills shelters the Dão from the Atlantic weather on its western side?
questions.exp: The Serra do Caramulo and the Buçaco hills stand between the Dão and the coast; the Estrela lies to the south-east. The Marão shelters the Douro, and Montejunto the Alenquer vineyards of Lisboa.

questions.q: Jaen of the Dão is the same grape as which Spanish variety?
questions.exp: Jaen is Mencía, the fragrant red of Bierzo and Galicia, early ripening and supple in a Dão blend. Tempranillo is Tinta Roriz in Portugal and Godello is Gouveio; Garnacha is barely grown in the Dão.

questions.q: Which Vinho Regional covers the territory of the Dão?
questions.exp: Terras do Dão, lands of the Dão, is the IGP that surrounds the DOC and takes wines made outside its grape list. Beira Atlântico is Bairrada's IGP and Terras da Beira lies to the east.

questions.q: Which city sits at the centre of the Dão plateau and houses its regional commission?
questions.exp: Viseu is the cathedral city at the centre of the plateau; the seven sub-regions lie around it, and Nelas, Mangualde, Tondela and Seia are the smaller towns a label may name.

questions.q: In which year was the Dão demarcated?
questions.exp: The Dão was demarcated in 1908, the same year as Vinho Verde, Colares and Carcavelos. 1756 is the Douro's date, 1979 Bairrada's, and 1986 the year Portugal joined the European Community.

questions.q: Which red grape is traditionally claimed to have originated in the Dão?
questions.exp: Touriga Nacional's name is tied to the village of Tourigo near Tondela, and the Dão claims it as a native though the Douro made it famous. Alicante Bouschet is a French crossing, Trincadeira the Alentejo's grape, and Tinta Barroca the Douro's.

questions.q: How many sub-regions does DOC Dão contain?
questions.exp: Seven: Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara and Terras de Senhorim. Vinho Verde, by contrast, has nine.

regions.name: Bairrada
regions.summary: Bairrada lies on the flat coastal plain between the hills of the Dão and the Atlantic, around Anadia and Mealhada, on the heavy clay, barro, that gives it its name, over limestone, with sand nearer the sea. Demarcated in 1979, it is the home of Baga, a late, small-berried red of high acid and high tannin that makes tart, tobacco-scented wines which age for decades and are often called the Nebbiolo of the Atlantic. It is also Portugal's sparkling capital: traditional method espumante from Baga, Bical and Maria Gomes, poured with the roast suckling pig of Mealhada. The rules were opened in 2003 to other grapes, and Clássico marks the traditional Baga-led wine. The IGP is Beira Atlântico.

terroir.climate: Maritime and cool, the Atlantic twenty kilometres to the west and nothing in between to stop it: mild winters, warm rather than hot summers, sea fog and breezes, and rainfall around 1,000 millimetres with a share of it in autumn, which is Baga's trial, because the grape ripens late and its tight bunches rot in a wet October. The climate makes the acidity that the sparkling wines and the long-lived reds depend on.
terroir.soils: Heavy clay, the barro of the name, over limestone on the gentle rises: cold, water-holding, late-warming soils that suit Baga's structure. Towards the coast the soil turns to sand, which gives lighter, earlier reds and whites and, at one famous site, allowed ungrafted vines to survive. The clay-limestone and the sand are the region's two schools.
terroir.topography: Low and open: a plain and gentle hills between 40 and 120 metres, running south from the Vouga near Aveiro to the Mondego at Coimbra, with the Caramulo and the Buçaco hills rising to the east. Vineyards share the land with olives, maize and the pine of the dunes; there is nothing steep anywhere.
terroir.water: The Atlantic sets the climate, and the Ria de Aveiro lagoon to the north-west adds damp air. The Cértima, Bairrada's own small river, drains the plain into the Pateira de Fermentelos lagoon; the Vouga bounds the north and the Mondego the south. The spa waters of Luso and Curia are the other famous liquids of the region.

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.styles: The grape of the region: small, thick-skinned berries in tight bunches, late ripening, high in acid and tannin, giving tart cherry, plum skin, tobacco and earth, hard when young and glorious at twenty years; also the base of rosé and blanc de noirs sparkling.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Allowed in the blend and welcome in a Clássico as a softener and perfume beside Baga.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.styles: A traditional partner that brings colour and soft fruit to a Baga blend.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: A traditional variety of the sandier soils, fruity and supple, in blends.

grapes.name: Camarate
grapes.styles: An old local red of the traditional list, soft and early, for blends.

grapes.name: Maria Gomes
grapes.styles: Fernão Pires under its Bairrada name: aromatic, soft, early ripening, the base of much white and sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Bical
grapes.styles: The region's finest white, early and crisp, with citrus and a waxy texture that ages; the backbone of the best sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: Acidity and lemon for the still and sparkling whites.

grapes.name: Cercial
grapes.styles: A high-acid white of the Beiras for the blends; not Madeira's Sercial.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Permitted since the rules opened, mostly for sparkling wine and for modern white blends.

wines.note: At least half Baga with the traditional grapes: deep ruby turning garnet, tart cherry and plum skin, tobacco, dried herbs and earth, high acid and drying tannin that need years in bottle. Decant it and serve with roast kid, game, or the leitão if the guest likes a red.
The modern blend after 2003, Baga softened with Touriga Nacional, Syrah or Merlot: rounder, earlier, oak-touched, and easier by the glass.

Traditional method sparkling wine, white from Bical, Maria Gomes and Arinto, or rosé and blanc de noirs from Baga, bone dry and high in acid; the classic match for leitão à Bairrada, the roast suckling pig of Mealhada.
Still whites from Bical, Maria Gomes and Arinto, crisp and lemony, some barrel fermented; good with the coast's fish and salt cod.
Pale, sharp rosés from Baga, drunk young and cold.
A smaller, finer-boned Baga from the sandy soils near the coast, including a famous ungrafted planting; lighter in colour, earlier to drink, a study wine for the sand against clay lesson.

made.viticulture: Baga sets the terms. It buds early and ripens late, in October, with tight bunches of small, thick-skinned berries that rot in a wet autumn and never ripen if the vine is overcropped, so the whole art is getting the crop down and the canopy open: low cordons on wires, green harvesting, leaf pulling around the bunches, and a wait at the end of the season that can lose the year to rain. For most of the twentieth century the vineyard was planted for volume, Baga yielding hugely on the fertile clay and sold hard and thin, which is the origin of its rough reputation. The revival since the 1980s cut yields, picked riper, and chose sites: Baga on the clay-limestone for structure, lighter varieties and some Baga on the sand for finesse. Since 2003 Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Pinot Noir may be planted for the DOC, and some houses build their reds on them; the Clássico wines and the Baga specialists hold to the old grape. The sparkling houses pick early, in August and September, for acidity.
made.winemaking: The traditional red was fermented whole, stems and all, in open lagares or vats with long maceration, aged in large old casks of oak or chestnut and released tannic and acid to soften over ten or fifteen years. Modern Baga keeps the long life and loses the rawness: destemming or partial stems, cooler fermentation, softer extraction, a year or two in used French oak, and a late release. Sparkling wine has been made here since the 1890s and Bairrada was the first Portuguese region to be known for it: the traditional method, with the second fermentation in bottle and time on the lees, from Bical, Maria Gomes and Arinto for the whites and from Baga pressed quickly off its skins for the rosés and blancs de noirs. Some houses make a Baga rosé by a short maceration; a few make orange or amphora wines, but these are curiosities.

law.classification: Bairrada was demarcated in 1979 and is DOC Bairrada under its regional commission, with Vinho Regional Beira Atlântico as the IGP around it. The rule book was rewritten in 2003: before it Baga was compulsory as the majority of every red; since then the DOC admits Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Pinot Noir beside the traditional grapes, and a wine with Baga at the centre may be labelled Bairrada Clássico, which requires at least 50 per cent Baga with the rest from the traditional list of Alfrocheiro, Camarate, Castelão, Jaen and Touriga Nacional. The whites rest on Maria Gomes, Bical, Arinto and Cercial. Sparkling wine is a category of the DOC in its own right, made by the traditional method, and the region carries the usual national terms, Reserva and Garrafeira.
tiers: DOC Bairrada
The coastal plain demarcated in 1979: red, white, rosé and sparkling wine from the listed grapes, the reds since 2003 free to use international varieties.
Bairrada Clássico
The traditional red: at least 50 per cent Baga with the rest from Alfrocheiro, Camarate, Castelão, Jaen and Touriga Nacional.
Bairrada Espumante
Traditional method sparkling wine, white, rosé or blanc de noirs, the region's second signature.
Vinho Regional Beira Atlântico
The IGP of the coastal Beiras, for wines outside the DOC rules.
labels: A Baga-led red of the traditional grapes.
Brut, the usual dryness of the sparkling wine.
The ageing term: thirty months with twelve in bottle on a red, which the old Baga wines exceed by years.
Own-rooted, ungrafted vines, possible on the sand.
Old vines, often Baga on the clay.
The regional wine of the coastal Beiras.

places.name: Anadia
places.note: The town at the centre of the region, home of the viticulture station founded in the nineteenth century and of the wine museum; the clay-limestone hills around it hold the classic Baga vineyards.

places.name: Mealhada
places.note: The town on the old Lisbon road famous for leitão à Bairrada, roast suckling pig served along a strip of restaurants, with the region's sparkling wine poured beside it; the clay of Mealhada also grows serious Baga.

places.name: Cantanhede
places.note: The western municipality towards the coast, sandier and lighter in its wines, with a large co-operative and the Baga on sand that teaches the soil lesson.

places.name: Buçaco and Luso
places.note: The forested hill on the eastern edge, with the spa town of Luso beneath it, whose palace hotel has blended and bottled its own long-aged Bairrada and Dão wines for over a century.

places.name: Sangalhos
places.note: A village near Anadia that houses the cellars of the region's largest sparkling and brand houses, built on the limestone for cool storage.

places.name: Águeda and Oliveira do Bairro
places.note: The northern municipalities towards the Vouga and the Aveiro lagoon, part of the sparkling trade and of the volume vineyard.

producers.name: Luís Pato
producers.why: The house that championed Baga from the 1980s, with single-vineyard wines from clay and an ungrafted planting on sand, and that led the region's revival.

producers.name: Caves São João
producers.why: The traditional house whose Frei João reds, released after years in cask, showed how long Baga could live.

producers.name: Casa de Saima
producers.why: A Sangalhos estate making Baga the old way, trodden in lagar and aged in old wood, a reference for the classic style.

producers.name: Quinta das Bágeiras
producers.why: A family estate near Anadia prized for serious Baga and for sparkling wine with long lees ageing.

producers.name: Caves Aliança
producers.why: The Sangalhos house of 1927 that made Bairrada sparkling wine a national habit and carries a wide range of Portuguese regions.

producers.name: Caves Messias
producers.why: A large Mealhada house of sparkling wine, Baga reds and aged aguardente.

producers.name: Campolargo
producers.why: The modern estate that planted international grapes beside Baga and makes the case for the 2003 rules.

producers.name: Buçaco Palace
producers.why: The hotel whose Bussaco reds and whites, blended from Bairrada and Dão and aged for years, are a collector's curiosity.

Describe Baga: late, tight bunches, high acid, high tannin, tart cherry and tobacco, long-lived.
Know the second signature, traditional method sparkling wine, and its dish, leitão.
Know the date, 1979, the 2003 opening of the rules, and the Clássico label at 50 per cent Baga.
Name the whites: Bical, Maria Gomes (Fernão Pires), Arinto, Cercial.
Know the IGP, Beira Atlântico, and the place names Anadia and Mealhada.
traps: Bairrada is clay and limestone on a flat coastal plain; the Dão next door is granite at altitude.
Baga is thin in colour when overcropped and black when yields are low; the grape is not the problem, the yield is.
Maria Gomes is Fernão Pires, not a separate grape; Cercial is not Madeira's Sercial.
Since 2003 a plain Bairrada red may contain no Baga at all; only Clássico guarantees it.
